questions.stem: A physiologist records muscle activity at the lower esophageal sphincter of a resting subject and observes steady tension that persists for minutes to hours without rhythmic relaxation. This pattern of contraction primarily serves which function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Maintaining a closed barrier between regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Propelling a bolus aborally toward the rectum

explanation.summary: Tonic contractions are sustained (minutes to hours) contractions that maintain steady tension, ideally suited to sphincters that must remain closed to regulate compartmental flow.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states tonic contractions persist without significant relaxation and are concentrated at sphincters to maintain a baseline closed state, providing barrier maintenance between GI compartments.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Propelling a bolus aborally is a role of phasic contractions (peristalsis), not sustained tonic tone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mixing chyme with secretions is achieved by phasic segmentation, not by sustained tonic contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Segmentation waves are rhythmic phasic contractions driven by discrete electrical events, the opposite of sustained tonic tone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Accelerating gastric emptying requires phasic antral contractions; tonic sphincter tone actually restrains flow.

questions.stem: In a segment of small intestine, an investigator records rhythmic, intermittent contractions that are each driven by discrete bursts of electrical activity. This contraction pattern is best suited for which functional role?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maintaining reservoir tone in the fundus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Preventing retrograde flow while at rest

explanation.summary: Phasic contractions are rhythmic, intermittent contractions driven by discrete electrical events and are specialized for propelling and mixing luminal contents.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines phasic contractions as rhythmic and intermittent, well-suited for propelling or mixing luminal contents, and locates them in the esophageal body, caudad stomach, small intestine, and colon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sustained sphincter closure is a tonic function, not a rhythmic phasic one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reservoir tone of the orad stomach (fundus) is maintained by tonic contraction, not phasic activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Preventing retrograde flow at rest is achieved by resting tonic sphincter tone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Holding steady tension for hours describes tonic, not phasic, contraction.

questions.stem: When a person swallows, the lower esophageal sphincter relaxes to allow the bolus to pass into the stomach. Which pair of neurotransmitters released by vagal inhibitory neurons mediates this relaxation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acetylcholine and the tachykinin substance P

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide

explanation.summary: Swallow-induced LES relaxation is mediated by vagal inhibitory (NANC) neurons that release nitric oxide (NO) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states the LES relaxes in response to swallowing via vagal inhibitory neurons that release nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide, allowing food into the stomach.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylcholine and the tachykinin substance P are excitatory transmitters that contract, rather than relax, GI smooth muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Norepinephrine hyperpolarizes muscle but is a sympathetic transmitter (with neuropeptide Y), not the vagal mediator of swallow-induced LES relaxation described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serotonin enhances motility broadly and mast-cell histamine is not the mediator of LES relaxation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dopamine and somatostatin are not the neurotransmitters responsible for swallow-triggered LES relaxation.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids. Manometry shows incomplete lower esophageal sphincter relaxation with elevated resting pressure, and a barium swallow demonstrates 'bird's beak' tapering. Which mechanism best explains his findings?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of myenteric neurons that release NO and VIP

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fibrotic stricture from long-standing acid reflux

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter muscle

explanation.summary: Achalasia results from loss of inhibitory NANC myenteric neurons that normally release NO and VIP, so the LES cannot relax during swallowing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick attributes achalasia to loss of inhibitory NANC neurons in the myenteric plexus that release NO and VIP; without this signal the LES fails to relax, producing dysphagia to solids and liquids, elevated resting pressure, and 'bird's beak' tapering.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Frequent transient LES relaxations underlie GERD, which causes reflux, not failure of relaxation with dysphagia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parietal cell destruction causes achlorhydria/pernicious anemia, not impaired LES relaxation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A peptic stricture from reflux causes mechanical narrowing but not the incomplete relaxation/elevated pressure pattern of loss of inhibitory neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyloric hypertrophy affects gastric outlet, not lower esophageal sphincter relaxation.

questions.stem: A patient experiences frequent episodes of acid reflux that occur without any swallowing. Resting lower esophageal sphincter pressure is measured and found to be normal. Which mechanism best accounts for the reflux?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of LES relaxation during swallowing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of NANC inhibitory myenteric neurons

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronically low resting LES tone since birth

choices.label: E
choices.text: Absent primary peristalsis in the esophagus

explanation.summary: GERD results from abnormally frequent transient LES relaxations (TLESRs), which permit reflux without a swallowing trigger, rather than from chronically low resting tone.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states GERD results from abnormally frequent transient LES relaxations, not from chronically low resting tone, allowing acid reflux without a swallowing trigger.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failure of LES relaxation during swallowing describes achalasia, which impairs bolus passage, not reflux.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of NANC inhibitory neurons produces achalasia, the opposite functional problem.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick explicitly notes GERD is not from chronically low resting tone, and resting pressure here is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absent primary peristalsis is not the described mechanism; the defect is inappropriate transient relaxation of the LES.

questions.stem: GI smooth muscle exhibits spontaneous rhythmic electrical activity even without direct neural stimulation. Which specialized cells generate the slow-wave oscillations that set the basal tempo of phasic contractions?

explanation.summary: Interstitial cells of Cajal (ICCs) are the pacemaker cells that generate slow waves (the basic electrical rhythm) setting the tempo of GI phasic contractions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies ICCs, located in the myenteric plexus and smooth muscle layers, as the pacemaker cells generating slow waves that set the tempo of phasic contractions throughout the gut.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mucosal enterochromaffin cells secrete serotonin; they do not generate the pacemaker slow waves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acid-secreting parietal cells produce gastric acid and have no pacemaker role.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucus-secreting goblet cells are unrelated to electrical rhythm generation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatic alpha motor neurons drive skeletal muscle at the neuromuscular junction, not GI smooth-muscle pacemaking.

questions.stem: In the gastric corpus, ICC-generated slow waves alone produce only weak contractions. According to the gating model of GI smooth muscle, a strong phasic contraction requires which additional event?

explanation.summary: Slow waves set the ceiling frequency and gate firing, but strong contractions require action potentials (spikes) superimposed on the slow-wave plateau.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states slow waves alone may produce only weak contractions and that strong phasic contractions require superimposed action potentials, which the slow wave gates.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gap junctions are needed for coordinated spread; losing them would impair, not strengthen, contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sympathetic input hyperpolarizes and decreases contraction, moving the slow wave away from threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chloride flux participates in generating slow waves themselves, not in driving the additional spikes needed for strong contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sphincter relaxation is a separate event and does not generate contractile force in the corpus.

questions.stem: An investigator records the basic electrical rhythm from the stomach of a healthy subject and finds it sets the pace of gastric peristalsis. Approximately how many slow waves per minute do gastric ICCs generate?

explanation.summary: In the stomach, ICCs generate approximately 3 slow waves per minute, setting the pace for gastric peristalsis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states ICCs in the stomach generate approximately 3 slow waves per minute, versus about 12/min in the duodenum and 8/min in the ileum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 12/min is the duodenal slow-wave frequency, not gastric.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About 8/min is the ileal slow-wave frequency, not gastric.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 20/min exceeds any normal GI slow-wave rate described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 1/min is below the stated gastric rate of about 3/min.

questions.stem: When the wall of the small intestine is distended by a bolus, the enteric nervous system contracts the circular muscle oral to the bolus and relaxes the circular muscle anal to it, propelling content aborally. This coordinated response is known as which reflex?

explanation.summary: The peristaltic reflex (law of the intestine) uses ascending excitation oral to the bolus and descending inhibition anal to it to propel content aborally.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes exactly this pattern—ascending excitatory contraction oral to the bolus and descending inhibitory relaxation anal to it—as the peristaltic reflex, also called the law of the intestine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Segmentation is non-propagating localized mixing without directional coordination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Haustration is the non-propagating colonic mixing pattern, not the directional propulsive reflex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mass movements are infrequent high-amplitude propagating colonic contractions, not the local distension reflex described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The migrating motor complex is the interdigestive fasting housekeeping program, not the bolus-triggered reflex.

questions.stem: During the postprandial state, the small intestine displays localized, non-propagating contractions at multiple points that repeatedly divide and mix the chyme without net forward movement. What is the primary functional purpose of this activity?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Expulsion of feces from the rectum

explanation.summary: Segmentation maximizes contact between chyme and the mucosa, serving digestion and absorption during the postprandial phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states segmentation serves digestion and absorption by maximizing contact between chyme and the intestinal mucosa, and predominates postprandially to slow transit for absorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rapid aboral propulsion is the role of peristalsis, not non-directional segmentation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Barrier maintenance is a tonic sphincter function, unrelated to segmentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Compartmental barriers are held by tonic contraction, not by mixing segments.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fecal expulsion involves colonic mass movements and the defecation reflex, not small-bowel segmentation.

questions.stem: In the colon, localized non-propagating contractions of the circular muscle occur within the sacculations formed by the teniae coli, mixing contents and facilitating water absorption without net directionality. These are termed which contractions?

explanation.summary: Haustral contractions are the colon's non-propagating mixing contractions within the haustra, facilitating water absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes haustral contractions as localized, non-propagating contractions within the sacculations that mix and expose colonic contents to the mucosa for water absorption, with no net directionality.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mass movements are the infrequent high-amplitude propagating (propulsive) colonic contractions, the opposite of haustral mixing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peristaltic waves are directional propulsive contractions, not the non-propagating haustral pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The migrating motor complex is an interdigestive fasting program of the stomach and small intestine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The described pattern is colonic haustration, not ileal segmentation.

questions.stem: A physiologist studies which colonic motor pattern accomplishes forward propulsion of stool. Which pattern provides this propulsive role through infrequent, high-amplitude propagating contractions?

explanation.summary: Mass movements are infrequent, high-amplitude propagating contractions that serve the propulsive role in the colon.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines mass movements as infrequent, high-amplitude propagating contractions that serve the propulsive role in the colon and are distinct from haustral contractions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Haustral contractions are non-propagating and mix rather than propel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tonic contractions maintain sustained tension (e.g., sphincters), not propulsion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Segmentation mixes content without net forward movement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phase I quiescence is a phase of the MMC with minimal activity, not colonic propulsion.

questions.stem: A patient on chronic oral opioids for pain develops constipation with hard stools and no evidence of mechanical obstruction. Activation of mu-opioid receptors on myenteric neurons produces this effect primarily by which action?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stimulating the descending inhibitory motor pathway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blocking water reabsorption in the colon

explanation.summary: Mu-opioid receptors on myenteric neurons suppress acetylcholine release, blunting the ascending excitatory limb of the peristaltic reflex and slowing transit.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states mu-opioid receptors on myenteric neurons suppress acetylcholine release, blunting the ascending excitatory limb of the peristaltic reflex, producing slowed transit, increased water reabsorption, and constipation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Opioids suppress, not increase, acetylcholine release from these neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Stimulating descending inhibition is not the described mechanism; opioids blunt the ascending excitatory limb.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opioids reduce propulsive motility; they do not enhance mass movements.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Slowed transit increases water reabsorption; opioids do not block colonic water reabsorption.

questions.stem: A drug is given to a patient with opioid-induced constipation and relieves the constipation while leaving the patient's pain control intact. This agent belongs to which class?

explanation.summary: Methylnaltrexone is a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist (PAMORA) that reverses GI opioid effects without reversing central analgesia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that because the relevant receptors are peripheral (ENS), PAMORAs such as methylnaltrexone reverse GI opioid effects without reversing analgesia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A D2 antagonist (metoclopramide) is a prokinetic for gastroparesis, not the agent that spares analgesia in opioid constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A motilin agonist (erythromycin) stimulates gastric emptying but is not the described opioid-reversal agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A non-absorbable antibiotic (rifaximin) treats bacterial overgrowth, not opioid constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 5-HT4 agonist is a prokinetic but not the peripheral opioid antagonist described.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing diabetes develops postprandial nausea, vomiting, and early satiety, and gastric emptying is delayed without any mechanical obstruction. Which cellular change most likely underlies this presentation?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of interstitial cells of Cajal

explanation.summary: Diabetic gastroparesis results from chronic hyperglycemia damaging ICCs in the gastric antrum, disrupting slow-wave generation and delaying emptying without obstruction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states chronic hyperglycemia damages ICCs in the gastric antrum, disrupting slow wave generation and producing delayed gastric emptying without mechanical obstruction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pyloric hypertrophy causes mechanical outlet obstruction, which is explicitly absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastroparesis reflects impaired pacemaking, not excess motilin; motilin agonists are in fact used to treat it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parietal cell loss affects acid secretion, not gastric pacemaker-driven emptying.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ICC loss reduces or disorganizes slow-wave activity; it does not increase slow-wave frequency.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic gastroparesis is started on a first-line prokinetic agent to accelerate gastric emptying. By which mechanism does this drug act?

explanation.summary: Metoclopramide, a D2 receptor antagonist with prokinetic action, is the first-line pharmacologic management for diabetic gastroparesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick names metoclopramide, a D2 receptor antagonist with prokinetic action that accelerates gastric emptying, as first-line pharmacologic management of diabetic gastroparesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Motilin receptor agonism describes erythromycin, an alternative agent, not the first-line D2 antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Peripheral mu-opioid antagonism describes methylnaltrexone for opioid constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Muscarinic blockade would reduce, not enhance, GI motility.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chloride channel activation is not the mechanism of the first-line prokinetic described.

questions.stem: Between meals in a fasting individual, a distinct cyclical pattern of motor activity sweeps through the stomach and small intestine, clearing residual content and preventing bacterial overgrowth. This 'housekeeper' pattern is called what?

explanation.summary: The migrating motor complex (MMC) is the interdigestive 'housekeeper' that sweeps the stomach and small intestine during fasting, preventing bacterial overgrowth.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the MMC as a cyclical interdigestive pattern that sweeps the lumen clean between meals, serving as the gut's housekeeper and preventing bacterial overgrowth.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The gastrocolic reflex links gastric filling to colonic activity and is not the fasting housekeeping sweep.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The peristaltic reflex is a local distension-triggered propulsive response, not the cyclical fasting program.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Segmentation predominates postprandially for absorption, whereas the MMC operates during fasting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Haustral shuttling is a colonic mixing pattern, not the interdigestive sweep of the stomach and small intestine.

questions.stem: During the migrating motor complex, one phase consists of intense, regular contractions occurring at maximum slow-wave frequency that propagate aborally, sweeping the lumen clean. Which phase is this defining feature of the MMC?

explanation.summary: Phase III (the activity front) is the defining feature of the MMC: intense, regular contractions at maximum slow-wave frequency that propagate aborally.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states Phase III consists of intense, regular contractions at maximum slow wave frequency propagating aborally, lasting 5–10 minutes, and is the defining and most clinically significant feature of the MMC.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Phase I is quiescence with minimal or no contractile activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phase II shows intermittent, irregular contractions, not the intense regular activity front.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phase IV is a brief transition back to Phase I.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The postprandial phase is the fed pattern of segmentation and peristalsis, not an MMC phase.

questions.stem: The hormone that peaks during fasting and initiates the intense contractile activity front of the migrating motor complex is secreted by which cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Parietal cells of the gastric body

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mo cells of the duodenum and jejunum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chief cells of the gastric glands

choices.label: E
choices.text: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets

explanation.summary: Motilin, which triggers MMC Phase III, is secreted by Mo cells (enteroendocrine cells) in the duodenum and jejunum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states motilin is secreted by Mo cells in the duodenum and jejunum, released cyclically during fasting with peak secretion coinciding with the onset of Phase III.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Parietal cells secrete gastric acid and intrinsic factor, not motilin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, not motilin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enterochromaffin-like cells secrete histamine to stimulate acid, not motilin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin, not the MMC-triggering hormone.

questions.stem: A macrolide antibiotic is used clinically as a prokinetic agent to stimulate gastric emptying in patients with gastroparesis. It accomplishes this by acting as an agonist at which receptor?

explanation.summary: Erythromycin, a macrolide antibiotic, is a motilin receptor agonist used as a prokinetic to stimulate gastric emptying.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states erythromycin, a macrolide antibiotic, is a well-known motilin receptor agonist used clinically as a prokinetic agent in gastroparesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: D2 receptor action describes metoclopramide (an antagonist), not the macrolide agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mu-opioid receptor activity relates to opioids and PAMORAs, not erythromycin's prokinetic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythromycin's prokinetic effect is via motilin receptors, not direct muscarinic agonism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 5-HT4 agonism describes other prokinetics; erythromycin acts at the motilin receptor.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: A researcher examining a segment of intestinal wall identifies a ganglionated nerve network situated between the longitudinal and circular smooth muscle layers. This network serves as the primary regulator of which gastrointestinal function?

explanation.summary: The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus lies between the longitudinal and circular muscle layers and is the primary regulator of GI motility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Its position between the two muscle layers allows it to coordinate contraction and relaxation of smooth muscle, producing peristalsis and segmentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mucosal secretion is regulated by the submucosal plexus, not the myenteric plexus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Local blood flow is controlled by the submucosal plexus, which lies in the submucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nutrient absorption is a function of enterocytes, not of a nerve plexus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hormone release into blood is the role of enteroendocrine cells, not the myenteric plexus.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Neurons of a plexus located in the submucosa innervate secretory glands, goblet cells, and enterocytes, modulating release of water, electrolytes, and mucus into the lumen. This plexus is primarily responsible for which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mucosal secretion and local blood flow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter

explanation.summary: The submucosal (Meissner's) plexus regulates mucosal secretion, epithelial transport, and local blood flow rather than motility.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because it sits in the submucosa and innervates glands and epithelial cells, it governs secretory and vascular responses of the mucosa.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Peristalsis is coordinated by the myenteric plexus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sphincter relaxation is a motility function of the myenteric plexus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Segmentation is a motility pattern controlled by the myenteric plexus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Contraction of the muscularis externa is driven by the myenteric plexus.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: A term neonate fails to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life and develops bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. Rectal suction biopsy shows absent ganglion cells in the distal colon. Which mechanism best explains the obstruction?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypertrophy of the circular muscle layer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overproduction of serotonin by enteric EC cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of the internal anal sphincter to contract

explanation.summary: Hirschsprung disease results from an aganglionic distal segment that lacks inhibitory motor neurons, so it cannot relax.
explanation.whyCorrect: Without enteric inhibitory neurons, the aganglionic segment remains tonically contracted, producing functional obstruction and proximal dilation (megacolon).

whyWrongByChoice.B: The segment lacks neurons entirely; there is no excess parasympathetic drive causing spasm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypertrophy of the circular muscle describes pyloric stenosis, not Hirschsprung disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serotonin overproduction by enteric EC cells characterizes carcinoid syndrome, not aganglionosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The problem is failure of the aganglionic segment to relax, not a failure to contract.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: A neonate with failure to pass meconium is found to have an aganglionic distal colonic segment. This condition results from failure of which developmental process?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neural crest cell migration to the distal colon

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds

explanation.summary: Hirschsprung disease is caused by failure of neural crest cell migration, leaving the distal colon without ganglia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enteric ganglia derive from neural crest cells that migrate craniocaudally; arrest of this migration leaves the distal (rectosigmoid) colon aganglionic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failed duodenal recanalization causes duodenal atresia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Abnormal midgut rotation produces malrotation and predisposes to volvulus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Abnormal pancreatic bud fusion produces annular pancreas or pancreas divisum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Persistence of the vitelline duct produces a Meckel diverticulum.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Distension of the small intestinal wall triggers a reflex contained entirely within the enteric nervous system. Which sequence correctly describes this reflex arc?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intrinsic sensory neuron then interneuron then motor neuron

choices.label: B
choices.text: Motor neuron then interneuron then intrinsic sensory neuron

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intrinsic sensory neuron then motor neuron then interneuron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interneuron then intrinsic sensory neuron then motor neuron

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preganglionic neuron then spinal cord then motor neuron

explanation.summary: The ENS short-loop reflex flows from intrinsic sensory neurons (IPANs) to interneurons to motor neurons.
explanation.whyCorrect: IPANs detect the stimulus, interneurons integrate and distribute the signal, and motor neurons drive the effector response, all within the gut wall.

whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the arc; sensory neurons detect the stimulus first, not last.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interneurons integrate signals before motor output; motor neurons do not precede interneurons.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interneurons cannot begin the arc; sensory detection must come first.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A pathway routed through the spinal cord is a long-loop reflex, not the short-loop ENS reflex.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Intrinsic primary afferent neurons detect luminal distension and transmit signals to downstream enteric neurons. Which neurotransmitter do these sensory neurons most notably release?

explanation.summary: IPANs release acetylcholine (along with substance P) onto interneurons and motor neurons.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies acetylcholine as the most notable neurotransmitter released by activated IPANs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Norepinephrine is released by sympathetic postganglionic fibers, not intrinsic sensory neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.B: VIP is used by descending interneurons and inhibitory motor neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nitric oxide is released by inhibitory motor neurons to cause relaxation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatostatin is not the primary transmitter of IPANs.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Mechanical distension and luminal chemicals stimulate the most abundant enteroendocrine cell subtype to release a mediator from its basolateral surface that activates intrinsic primary afferent neurons. Which mediator is released?

explanation.summary: Enterochromaffin (EC) cells, the most abundant EEC subtype, release serotonin (5-HT) that acts on IPANs.
explanation.whyCorrect: EC cells detect mechanical and chemical stimuli and release 5-HT basolaterally onto IPANs to initiate peristaltic and secretomotor reflexes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastrin is released by antral G cells, not EC cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Histamine is released by enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells to amplify acid secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CCK is released by duodenal I cells and acts mainly on pancreas, gallbladder, and vagal afferents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secretin is released by duodenal S cells in response to acid.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Ahead of an advancing bolus, inhibitory enteric motor neurons produce smooth muscle relaxation. Which combination of neurotransmitters mediates this relaxation?

explanation.summary: Inhibitory motor neurons release nitric oxide, VIP (and ATP) to relax smooth muscle ahead of the bolus.
explanation.whyCorrect: These transmitters produce receptive relaxation aboral to the bolus, complementing ascending excitation during the peristaltic reflex.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acetylcholine and substance P are released by excitatory motor neurons to cause contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Norepinephrine and epinephrine are catecholamines of the sympathetic system, not enteric motor transmitters.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serotonin and histamine are not the relaxation transmitters of enteric motor neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gastrin and CCK are gut hormones, not enteric motor neuron transmitters.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: During peristalsis, the segment oral to a bolus contracts while the segment aboral to it relaxes. This coordination reflects which arrangement of enteric interneuron activity?

explanation.summary: The peristaltic reflex is built on ascending excitation (contraction behind the bolus) and descending inhibition (relaxation ahead of it).
explanation.whyCorrect: Ascending interneurons drive excitatory motor neurons orally, and descending interneurons activate inhibitory motor neurons aborally, propelling contents forward.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This reverses the pattern; contraction occurs orally and relaxation aborally.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Without descending inhibition the gut ahead of the bolus could not relax to receive it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Without ascending excitation there would be no propulsive contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the correct direction of excitation and inhibition.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: During a fight-or-flight response, sympathetic fibers release norepinephrine onto enteric neurons. What is the expected net effect on the GI tract?

explanation.summary: Sympathetic activation is net inhibitory: it decreases motility, reduces secretion, and contracts sphincters.
explanation.whyCorrect: Norepinephrine suppresses excitatory ENS output, slowing propulsion and closing sphincters as blood is redirected away from the gut.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased motility and secretion is the parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sympathetic activity contracts, not relaxes, sphincters.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sympathetic activity does reduce secretion but contracts sphincters rather than relaxing them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sympathetic activity reduces secretion but also reduces motility rather than leaving it unchanged.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers to the GI tract originate in the thoracolumbar spinal cord and synapse before reaching the gut wall. Where do these fibers synapse?

explanation.summary: Sympathetic preganglionic fibers (T5-L2) synapse in prevertebral ganglia (celiac, superior and inferior mesenteric).
explanation.whyCorrect: Postganglionic fibers then project from these prevertebral ganglia to the ENS, where they release norepinephrine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dorsal root ganglia contain somatic sensory cell bodies, not sympathetic synapses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The myenteric plexus is a target of postganglionic fibers, not the preganglionic synapse site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The submucosal plexus is likewise a target, not the site of the preganglionic synapse.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The nodose ganglion contains vagal (parasympathetic) afferent cell bodies.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Norepinephrine released by sympathetic fibers suppresses acetylcholine release from enteric neurons, producing a 'braking' effect on motility. This effect is mediated primarily by which receptor?

explanation.summary: Norepinephrine acts on alpha-2 adrenergic receptors on ENS neurons to suppress excitatory transmitter release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alpha-2 receptors on enteric neurons inhibit acetylcholine release, decreasing motility and secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-2 receptors are not the receptor mediating the sympathetic braking of the ENS described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M3 muscarinic receptors mediate excitatory cholinergic effects, not sympathetic inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nicotinic cholinergic receptors mediate fast excitatory transmission at ganglia, including parasympathetic input.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Histaminergic H2 receptors mediate gastric acid secretion, unrelated to adrenergic braking.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: The distal colon, rectum, and internal anal sphincter receive parasympathetic innervation from which source?

explanation.summary: The distal colon, rectum, and internal anal sphincter receive parasympathetic input from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4).
explanation.whyCorrect: Vagal supply reaches only to the proximal colon; the hindgut-derived distal structures are supplied by sacral parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic) fibers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The vagus supplies the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and proximal colon only.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The greater splanchnic nerve carries sympathetic, not parasympathetic, fibers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The superior mesenteric ganglion is a sympathetic prevertebral ganglion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm, not the distal colon.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Vagal parasympathetic fibers synapse on enteric neurons and release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors. Activation of this pathway produces which effect on the GI tract?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduced motility with tonic sphincter contraction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sphincter contraction with increased mucus secretion

explanation.summary: Parasympathetic activation is broadly excitatory: increased motility, increased secretion, and sphincter relaxation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vagal input amplifies intrinsic ENS circuits, enhancing propulsion and secretion while relaxing sphincters to allow passage of contents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reduced motility with tonic sphincter contraction describes the sympathetic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Parasympathetic activity increases, not reduces, secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parasympathetic activity relaxes rather than contracts sphincters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Parasympathetic activity increases rather than reduces motility.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: A patient historically undergoes surgical cutting of the vagus nerve to treat peptic ulcer disease. Which effect on gastric physiology is expected?

explanation.summary: Vagotomy reduces gastric acid secretion and motility by removing parasympathetic excitatory input.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vagus drives parietal cell acid output and gastric motility; cutting it lowers both, which is why it was used to treat ulcers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vagotomy decreases, not increases, acid and motility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reduced acid is expected, but vagotomy does not primarily increase mucus secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acid is reduced and motility decreased, not unchanged and increased.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vagal stimulation normally raises gastrin; vagotomy would reduce vagal-driven gastrin release.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Before food reaches the stomach, the sight and smell of a meal initiate gastric acid secretion. Which pathway mediates this preparatory phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sympathetic fibers acting directly on parietal cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulating secretin from duodenal S cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gastrin alone acting without neural input

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vagus activating enteric neurons and parietal cells

explanation.summary: The cephalic phase is neural and vagally mediated: the vagus activates ENS neurons and parietal cells to secrete acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sensory stimuli activate the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, which drives ENS neurons, parietal cells, and G cells before food arrives.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sympathetic input inhibits, rather than initiates, gastric secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Secretin acts during the intestinal phase and inhibits gastric acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastrin contributes, but the cephalic phase requires vagal neural input, not gastrin alone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CCK is an intestinal-phase hormone, not the initiator of the cephalic phase.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Sham-feeding experiments, in which subjects chew and spit food without swallowing, are used to study cephalic-phase acid secretion. This secretion is abolished by which intervention?

explanation.summary: Cephalic-phase acid secretion is entirely vagally mediated and is abolished by vagotomy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sham feeding confirms the cephalic phase depends on vagal outflow; cutting the vagus eliminates it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PPIs reduce acid output in all phases but do not abolish the cephalic neural drive itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antrectomy removes the gastrin source but does not eliminate the vagal cephalic pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatostatin broadly suppresses secretion but is not the intervention shown to abolish the cephalic phase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: H2 blockade reduces histamine-driven acid downstream but does not abolish vagal cephalic signaling.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: During the cephalic phase, vagally activated enteric neurons in the gastric antrum release a peptide that stimulates G cells to secrete gastrin. Which peptide is this?

explanation.summary: ENS neurons release gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP) onto antral G cells to stimulate gastrin secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vagal activation to ENS GRP to gastrin loop is a potent neuro-hormonal stimulus for acid secretion during the cephalic phase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: VIP is an inhibitory transmitter that relaxes smooth muscle, not a stimulus for gastrin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Somatostatin inhibits gastrin release rather than stimulating it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secretin is released by duodenal S cells and inhibits gastric acid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Substance P is an excitatory motor transmitter, not the G-cell stimulating peptide.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Specialized epithelial cells scattered throughout the GI mucosa express chemosensory receptors on their apical surface and release hormones in response to luminal nutrients. What is the primary role of these cells?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Detect luminal nutrients and release hormones

choices.label: D
choices.text: Absorb the bulk of dietary nutrients

choices.label: E
choices.text: Provide structural support to intestinal villi

explanation.summary: Enteroendocrine cells act as luminal sensory transducers, detecting nutrients and releasing hormones.
explanation.whyCorrect: Apical chemosensory GPCRs let EECs sense chyme composition and translate it into neural and hormonal signals coordinating digestion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Smooth muscle contraction is driven by excitatory motor neurons, not EECs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Slow-wave pacemaker activity is generated by interstitial cells of Cajal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bulk nutrient absorption is performed by enterocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Structural support is not the function of enteroendocrine cells.

questions.topicName: Neural Control of the GI System (Enteric Nervous System)
questions.stem: Excitatory enteric motor neurons act on gastrointestinal smooth muscle to produce contraction. Which neurotransmitters do these neurons release?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vasoactive intestinal peptide and nitric oxide

explanation.summary: Excitatory motor neurons release acetylcholine and substance P onto smooth muscle to cause contraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: These are the classic excitatory transmitters that increase the contractile state of gut smooth muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nitric oxide and ATP are released by inhibitory motor neurons to cause relaxation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: VIP and nitric oxide mediate relaxation, not contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Norepinephrine and neuropeptide Y are sympathetic transmitters, not enteric excitatory motor transmitters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serotonin and CCK are signaling mediators, not the transmitters of excitatory motor neurons.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman undergoes upper endoscopy with biopsy of the gastric body. Histology highlights large eosinophilic cells within the oxyntic glands that secrete hydrochloric acid and a glycoprotein required for vitamin B12 uptake. Which cell type is described?

explanation.summary: Parietal (oxyntic) cells secrete both HCl and intrinsic factor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Parietal cells are the only gastric cell that secretes hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor; the glycoprotein needed for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum is intrinsic factor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase, not acid or intrinsic factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ECL cells secrete histamine, a paracrine stimulant of acid secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: G cells secrete gastrin, an endocrine hormone released into blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: D cells secrete somatostatin, an inhibitory paracrine peptide.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: A patient who has undergone total gastrectomy can no longer produce intrinsic factor. Absorption of which nutrient is most impaired as a result?

explanation.summary: Intrinsic factor is required for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intrinsic factor secreted by parietal cells binds vitamin B12 and is required for its absorption in the terminal ileum; its loss causes B12 deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folate absorption does not depend on intrinsic factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin C is absorbed independently of gastric intrinsic factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium absorption is not intrinsic factor-dependent, though gastric acid aids solubility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K absorption relies on bile and does not require intrinsic factor.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: Biopsy of the gastric fundus shows basophilic cells at the base of the oxyntic glands filled with apical zymogen granules. Which product do these cells secrete?

explanation.summary: Chief (zymogenic) cells store and secrete pepsinogen in apical granules.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chief cells located in the base of oxyntic glands store pepsinogen and gastric lipase in apical secretory granules; pepsinogen is the inactive precursor of pepsin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Histamine is secreted by ECL cells, not zymogen-granule-containing chief cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastrin is secreted by antral G cells into the bloodstream.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Somatostatin is secreted by D cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: Antral mucosal biopsy identifies enteroendocrine cells that sense luminal peptides and release a hormone into the blood that stimulates gastric acid secretion. Which cell type is this?

explanation.summary: Antral G cells sense luminal peptides/amino acids and release gastrin into the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: G cells are enteroendocrine cells concentrated in the antrum that sense luminal peptides and amino acids and release gastrin into the bloodstream to stimulate parietal cell acid secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Parietal cells respond to gastrin but secrete acid, not a blood-borne stimulatory hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, not gastrin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ECL cells release histamine as a paracrine, not endocrine, signal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: D cells release somatostatin, which inhibits acid secretion.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: In the gastric body, one cell type releases the dominant paracrine stimulant that drives parietal cell acid secretion. Which cell type secretes this substance?

explanation.summary: Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells secrete histamine, the dominant paracrine stimulant of parietal cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: ECL cells in the gastric body/fundus release histamine, which the brick identifies as the dominant paracrine stimulant of parietal cell acid secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase, not histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: G cells secrete gastrin, an endocrine hormone, not the dominant paracrine drive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D cells secrete somatostatin, which inhibits rather than stimulates acid secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mucous neck cells secrete mucus and bicarbonate for protection.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: A paracrine cell located in both the gastric antrum and body releases a peptide that inhibits gastrin release and acid secretion, especially when luminal pH falls. Which product does this cell secrete?

explanation.summary: D cells secrete somatostatin, an inhibitor of gastrin release and acid secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Somatostatin from D cells suppresses gastrin release from G cells and directly inhibits parietal cell acid secretion; it is released in response to low luminal pH.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Histamine stimulates, rather than inhibits, acid secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastrin stimulates acid secretion and is the target of somatostatin's inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pepsinogen is a digestive zymogen, not an inhibitory paracrine signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intrinsic factor supports B12 absorption and does not regulate acid secretion.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: The apical H+/K+-ATPase of the parietal cell couples ATP hydrolysis to ion movement across the luminal membrane. Which function does this pump directly perform?

explanation.summary: The H+/K+-ATPase exchanges intracellular H+ for luminal K+, secreting H+ into the lumen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The apical proton pump uses ATP to exchange intracellular H+ for luminal K+ in a 1:1 ratio, directly secreting H+ into the gastric lumen to generate the acidic environment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbonic anhydrase generates H+ intracellularly but is a separate enzyme, not the pump.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Basolateral Cl- entry occurs via the Cl-/HCO3- exchanger, not the proton pump.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HCO3- export is performed by the basolateral Cl-/HCO3- antiporter.
whyWrongByChoice.E: K+ recycling occurs through apical K+ channels, not the ATPase itself.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: Shortly after a large meal, a healthy person shows a transient rise in venous blood and urine pH. Which parietal cell transport event most directly generates this alkaline load?

explanation.summary: The alkaline tide results from basolateral HCO3- efflux via the Cl-/HCO3- exchanger.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbonic anhydrase generates H+ and HCO3-; while H+ is secreted apically, HCO3- is exported into the blood via the basolateral Cl-/HCO3- antiporter, producing the postprandial alkaline tide.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Apical H+/K+ exchange secretes acid into the lumen, not base into the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Apical Cl- efflux contributes to luminal HCl formation, not blood alkalinization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: K+ recycling maintains pump substrate and does not alter blood pH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carbonic anhydrase is active, not inhibited, and supplies the HCO3- that is exported.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: Histamine stimulates parietal cell acid secretion by binding an H2 receptor that activates adenylyl cyclase. Which intracellular second messenger mediates this effect?

explanation.summary: The H2 receptor is a Gs-coupled GPCR that raises cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: Histamine binding the H2 receptor activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP, which activates PKA and drives H+/K+-ATPase translocation to the apical membrane.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IP3 is generated by the Gq/M3 and CCK-B pathways, not the H2 receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diacylglycerol arises from PLC activation, characteristic of M3/gastrin signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elevated Ca2+ is the mediator for ACh and gastrin, not for histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: cGMP is not the second messenger for the H2 receptor.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: Acetylcholine released from enteric neurons binds M3 muscarinic receptors on parietal cells, increasing acid output. Which second messenger mediates this response?

explanation.summary: M3 receptors activate PLC, raising IP3/DAG and intracellular Ca2+.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACh binding M3 receptors activates phospholipase C, generating IP3 and DAG and elevating intracellular Ca2+ (and PKC), which stimulates acid secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: cAMP is the messenger for the histamine H2 pathway, not M3.
whyWrongByChoice.B: cGMP is not involved in M3 parietal cell signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitric oxide is not the second messenger for muscarinic acid stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adenosine is not part of the M3 acid-secretory pathway.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: A gastrin analogue is used experimentally to stimulate parietal cell acid secretion. Gastrin exerts this effect by binding which receptor?

explanation.summary: Gastrin acts on CCK-B receptors on parietal and ECL cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastrin binds CCK-B receptors on parietal cells (direct stimulation) and ECL cells (triggering histamine release), signaling via increased intracellular Ca2+.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The H2 receptor is the target of histamine, not gastrin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The M3 receptor mediates acetylcholine, not gastrin, signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GRP receptors are on G cells and mediate vagal stimulation of gastrin release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gi-coupled receptors mediate somatostatin's inhibitory effect, not gastrin.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: In the gastric antrum, D cells increase secretion of their inhibitory peptide in response to a specific luminal change that provides negative feedback on acid production. Which change triggers this release?

explanation.summary: D cells release somatostatin in response to low (falling) luminal pH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Somatostatin release from D cells is triggered by low luminal pH, forming a negative feedback loop that suppresses gastrin release and acid secretion when the stomach becomes acidic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A rising (less acidic) pH removes the stimulus for somatostatin release.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Luminal peptides stimulate G-cell gastrin release, not D-cell somatostatin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antral distension favors gastrin/acid responses rather than somatostatin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acetylcholine inhibits somatostatin release from D cells.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: During the cephalic phase, the CNS initiates gastric acid secretion mainly through vagal release of a peptide that acts on antral G cells and is not blocked by atropine. Which peptide is this?

explanation.summary: GRP is the vagal, non-muscarinic mediator of gastrin release in the cephalic phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP) is released by antral enteric neurons under vagal input, binds GRP receptors on G cells, and triggers gastrin secretion; because it is non-muscarinic, its effect is not blocked by atropine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylcholine acts through muscarinic receptors and is blocked by atropine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Secretin inhibits gastric acid secretion and is a duodenal signal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatostatin inhibits gastrin and acid secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cholecystokinin is a duodenal hormone not central to cephalic-phase gastrin release.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: Pepsinogen secreted by chief cells must be converted to active pepsin before protein digestion can begin. Which luminal condition triggers this activation?

explanation.summary: Low luminal pH (below 5) cleaves pepsinogen to active pepsin.
explanation.whyCorrect: At luminal pH below 5 (optimally 1.8-3.5), H+ cleaves an inhibitory peptide from pepsinogen, exposing the active site; pepsin then autocatalytically activates additional pepsinogen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alkaline pH above 7 inactivates pepsin rather than activating pepsinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bile salts are duodenal and do not activate pepsinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elevated luminal K+ does not trigger pepsinogen activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bicarbonate secretion raises pH and would oppose activation.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: As chyme passes from the stomach into the duodenum, pepsin activity is irreversibly lost. Which condition is responsible for this inactivation?

explanation.summary: Pepsin is irreversibly inactivated at pH above 7 in the alkaline duodenum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pepsin activity is irreversibly lost at pH above 7, which occurs as acidic chyme is neutralized upon entering the alkaline duodenum, confining pepsin's proteolysis to the stomach.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Very low pH favors pepsin activity, not inactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pancreatic lipase digests fat and does not inactivate pepsin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bile acid binding does not account for irreversible pepsin inactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intrinsic factor relates to B12 absorption, not pepsin activity.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: Chief cells secrete an acid-stable enzyme, active at pH 3-6, that begins fat digestion within the stomach. Which reaction does this enzyme catalyze?

explanation.summary: Gastric lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides into fatty acids and diglycerides.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastric lipase, an acid-stable lipase active at pH 3-6, cleaves triglycerides into fatty acids and diglycerides, accounting for roughly 10-30% of total fat digestion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Peptide bond cleavage is performed by pepsin, not gastric lipase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Starch hydrolysis is carried out by amylases, not gastric lipase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Emulsification is a function of bile salts, not a gastric enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protein denaturation is driven by luminal acid, not by lipase.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: A patient with achlorhydria has markedly impaired gastric-phase protein digestion. What is the most direct cause of this impairment?

explanation.summary: Without acid, pepsinogen cannot be activated, eliminating the gastric phase of protein digestion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Achlorhydria removes the acidic environment needed to cleave pepsinogen into pepsin, so the gastric phase of protein digestion is lost; the small intestine only partially compensates via pancreatic proteases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pancreatic enzyme output is not primarily reduced by achlorhydria and actually helps compensate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of intrinsic factor affects B12 absorption, not protein digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reduced lipase affects fat, not protein, digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatostatin changes regulate acid secretion but do not directly block protein digestion.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: A patient develops autoantibodies that progressively destroy gastric parietal cells. Deficiency of which vitamin is most likely to result?

explanation.summary: Parietal cell destruction removes intrinsic factor, causing B12 malabsorption (pernicious anemia).
explanation.whyCorrect: Autoantibody destruction of parietal cells eliminates intrinsic factor secretion, causing vitamin B12 malabsorption and pernicious anemia, along with achlorhydria that impairs non-heme iron absorption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vitamin C absorption does not depend on parietal cell function.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate absorption is independent of intrinsic factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vitamin D absorption is not tied to parietal cell secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K absorption depends on bile, not intrinsic factor.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: The gastric epithelium is continuously exposed to concentrated HCl and pepsin yet is normally protected. Which mechanism is the primary defense layer against luminal acid?

explanation.summary: The mucus-bicarbonate barrier is the primary gastric mucosal defense.
explanation.whyCorrect: Surface mucous cells secrete an adherent mucus gel that traps bicarbonate, establishing a pH gradient from ~2 at the lumen to ~7 at the epithelial surface; this is the primary defense layer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tight junctions prevent H+ back-diffusion but are a supporting, not primary, layer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epithelial cell restitution reseals breaches after injury as a third-line mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastric mucosal blood flow supports defense but is not the primary barrier to acid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mast cell degranulation aggravates injury rather than protecting the mucosa.

questions.topicName: Gastric Secretion and the Parietal Cell
questions.stem: Chronic NSAID use predisposes to gastric ulcers by inhibiting COX-1 in the gastric mucosa. Reduction of which protective function is most directly responsible?

explanation.summary: COX-1 inhibition lowers prostaglandins that stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: COX-1 produces prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) that stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion and maintain mucosal blood flow; NSAIDs inhibit COX-1, weakening this defense and predisposing to ulceration.

whyWrongByChoice.B: NSAIDs do not act on the proton pump; reducing acid would protect, not harm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastrin signaling is not the mucosal defense impaired by NSAIDs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pepsinogen secretion is not the protective function NSAIDs impair.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intrinsic factor output is unrelated to NSAID-induced mucosal injury.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: A physiologist studies enteroendocrine cells in duodenal biopsies. One population releases its hormone when long-chain fatty acids and partially digested peptides contact its apical surface, and this hormone drives gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion. Which cell type is being described?

explanation.summary: I cells of the duodenum and proximal jejunum secrete cholecystokinin (CCK) in response to luminal fatty acids and peptides.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies I cells as the source of CCK, stimulated by long-chain fatty acids, peptides, and amino acids, producing enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: S cells secrete secretin in response to luminal acid, not fat/protein, and drive bicarbonate secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: K cells secrete GIP in response to glucose and fat and act on beta cells, not on the gallbladder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: G cells secrete gastrin and stimulate gastric acid; they are predominantly in the antrum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: D cells secrete somatostatin, an inhibitory hormone, not CCK.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: A segment of duodenal epithelium releases its hormone specifically when luminal pH falls below approximately 4.5 as acidic chyme arrives from the stomach, triggering neutralization of the duodenal contents. Which cell type secretes this hormone?

explanation.summary: S cells release secretin when luminal pH drops below ~4.5, a graded response to duodenal acidification.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states secretin is released from S cells of the duodenum and proximal jejunum when luminal pH falls below about 4.5, with acid as the dominant stimulus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: I cells respond to fatty acids and peptides and release CCK, not secretin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: K cells respond to glucose and fat and release GIP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: L cells respond to glucose and fat in the ileum/colon and release GLP-1 and PYY.
whyWrongByChoice.E: G cells release gastrin and are not triggered by luminal acidification in this manner.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: After a high-fat meal, an intestinal hormone is released that stimulates pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion. Beyond this action, which additional effect does the same hormone produce?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of insulin from beta cells

explanation.summary: CCK stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion AND causes gallbladder contraction to expel bile.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes CCK acting on gallbladder smooth muscle to cause contraction and bile expulsion into the common bile duct, complementing its pancreatic enzyme action.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CCK increases pyloric sphincter tone and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi; it does not relax the pyloric sphincter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CCK does not stimulate gastric acid; secretin actually inhibits acid output.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CCK slows gastric emptying rather than accelerating it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insulin potentiation is the action of GIP/GLP-1, not CCK.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: In response to acidic chyme, secretin triggers delivery of a large volume of alkaline, bicarbonate-rich fluid into the duodenum. Which cells are directly stimulated by secretin to produce this fluid?

explanation.summary: Secretin acts on pancreatic ductal cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich alkaline fluid.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states secretin binds receptors on pancreatic ductal cells, raising cAMP and driving CFTR-dependent bicarbonate secretion that neutralizes the duodenum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Parietal cells secrete acid; secretin inhibits them rather than stimulating bicarbonate output.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes under CCK, not the bicarbonate fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: I cells secrete CCK; they do not produce pancreatic bicarbonate fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gallbladder epithelium concentrates and stores bile, not pancreatic bicarbonate.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: Following a meal rich in glucose and fat, K cells of the duodenum and jejunum release a hormone that potentiates insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells, linking the intestinal phase to postprandial glucose handling. Which hormone is this?

explanation.summary: K cells secrete GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide), which potentiates insulin release.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists K cells secreting GIP in response to glucose and fat, with insulin release and gastric inhibition as key functions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CCK is released by I cells and targets the pancreas and gallbladder, not beta-cell insulin potentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Secretin drives bicarbonate secretion and acid inhibition, not insulin release.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gastrin stimulates gastric acid secretion from G cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Motilin regulates the migrating motor complex between meals; it is not the K-cell incretin.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: L cells located in the ileum and colon release their hormones in response to luminal glucose and fat. According to the brick, what is the primary function attributed to these hormones?

explanation.summary: L-cell hormones (GLP-1, PYY) regulate satiety and gut motility.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's table lists L cells in the ileum and colon secreting GLP-1 and PYY with satiety and motility regulation as their key function.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric acid secretion is stimulated by gastrin from G cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gallbladder smooth-muscle contraction is driven by CCK from I cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pancreatic digestive enzyme secretion is stimulated by CCK, not L-cell hormones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatic bicarbonate secretion is the function of secretin from S cells.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: A hormone-secreting cell type located predominantly in the gastric antrum releases a hormone whose principal action is stimulation of gastric acid secretion, with only a minor role in the intestinal phase. Which cell type is this?

explanation.summary: G cells, predominantly in the antrum, secrete gastrin, which stimulates gastric acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's table identifies G cells in the antrum secreting gastrin, whose key function is gastric acid stimulation with a minor intestinal role.

whyWrongByChoice.A: S cells secrete secretin and reside in the duodenum/proximal jejunum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: K cells secrete GIP and drive insulin release.
whyWrongByChoice.C: I cells secrete CCK for enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: L cells secrete GLP-1/PYY for satiety and motility.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: When acidic, hyperosmolar chyme distends the duodenum, mechanoreceptors and chemoreceptors in the duodenal wall signal the enteric nervous system, reducing antral contractions and increasing pyloric tone within seconds. What is this rapid neural mechanism called?

explanation.summary: The enterogastric reflex is the immediate neural brake slowing gastric emptying.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the enterogastric reflex: duodenal receptors detect distension, low pH, hyperosmolarity, or nutrients and signal the ENS to slow antral peristalsis and raise pyloric tone within seconds.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The gastrocolic reflex increases colonic motility after gastric filling, not a duodenal brake on emptying.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The gastroileal reflex promotes ileal emptying into the colon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The migrating motor complex sweeps the gut between meals, not a postprandial duodenal brake.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptive relaxation is fundic accommodation during swallowing, not duodenal feedback.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: A researcher measures gastric emptying after test meals composed of a single macronutrient. Which macronutrient present in the duodenum most potently slows gastric emptying?

explanation.summary: Fat is the most potent inhibitor of gastric emptying.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states fat is the most potent inhibitor of gastric emptying, with even small amounts triggering significant slowing, because fat requires the most digestive preparation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Protein has a moderate inhibitory effect, less than fat.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbohydrates such as glucose have the least inhibitory effect of the macronutrients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fiber is not identified as the dominant inhibitory signal in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Water empties rapidly and does not potently slow emptying.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: CCK stimulates the exocrine pancreas to release digestive enzymes and zymogens by binding a specific receptor on acinar cells. Which receptor mediates this action?

explanation.summary: CCK acts on acinar CCK-A receptors to stimulate enzyme secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick specifies CCK binds CCK-A receptors on acinar cells, stimulating secretion of digestive enzymes and zymogens into the pancreatic duct.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Secretin receptors are on ductal cells and mediate bicarbonate secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GIP receptors are on pancreatic beta cells and mediate insulin release.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Muscarinic M3 receptors mediate vagal cholinergic effects, not the CCK-specific acinar action described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Histamine H2 receptors are on gastric parietal cells and mediate acid secretion.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: Secretin binds its receptor on pancreatic ductal cells and activates an intracellular second messenger that drives the bicarbonate secretion machinery. Which second messenger is generated?

explanation.summary: Secretin raises intracellular cAMP in ductal cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states secretin binds ductal-cell receptors, activating adenylyl cyclase and raising intracellular cAMP, which drives CFTR-dependent bicarbonate secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IP3 mobilizes calcium in Gq-coupled pathways, not the secretin-cAMP mechanism described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcium is not the second messenger cited for secretin's ductal action.
whyWrongByChoice.D: cGMP is used by nitric oxide/natriuretic peptide signaling, not secretin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diacylglycerol activates protein kinase C in Gq pathways, not secretin's Gs-cAMP pathway.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: A patient's duodenal pH remains persistently below 4 because bicarbonate delivery is inadequate. Fat digestion fails and greasy, foul-smelling stools develop. Which pancreatic enzyme is most directly inactivated by this low pH?

explanation.summary: Lipase is irreversibly denatured at low duodenal pH, causing steatorrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states lipase is irreversibly denatured at pH below 4 and loses significant activity below pH 5, so impaired neutralization inactivates lipase and produces steatorrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amylase digests carbohydrate and is not the enzyme responsible for the fatty stools described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Trypsinogen is an inactive precursor; the brick highlights lipase as most acid-sensitive for fat digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pepsin is a gastric enzyme that actually works best at acidic pH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enterokinase is a brush-border enzyme that activates trypsinogen, not the fat-digesting enzyme denatured here.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: For bile and pancreatic juice to enter the duodenum together after a fatty meal, CCK acts on the muscular sphincter at the duodenal papilla. What effect does CCK have on the sphincter of Oddi?

explanation.summary: CCK relaxes the sphincter of Oddi to allow bile and pancreatic juice to enter the duodenum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states CCK relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, facilitating coordinated delivery of bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenal lumen while the gallbladder contracts.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased tone would obstruct, not facilitate, delivery of bile and juice.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sustained contraction would block the papilla against outflow.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rhythmic spasm is not the described action and would impede flow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Constriction would prevent the coordinated delivery CCK promotes.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: When undigested nutrients reach the distal small intestine, L cells release a hormone that produces a powerful inhibition of gastric emptying known as the 'ileal brake.' Which hormone mediates this effect?

explanation.summary: PYY from ileal L cells mediates the ileal brake, strongly slowing gastric emptying.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states PYY, released from L cells in the ileum, produces the 'ileal brake,' a powerful inhibition of gastric emptying when nutrients reach the distal small intestine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastrin stimulates gastric acid, not the ileal brake.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Motilin drives interdigestive motility, not the postprandial ileal brake.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Secretin slows motility via antral inhibition but is not the ileal-brake hormone released distally.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GIP contributes to gastric inhibition but the ileal brake is specifically attributed to PYY.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: Glands located in the submucosa of the proximal duodenum secrete alkaline mucus in response to acid and secretin stimulation, helping protect the mucosa from acidic chyme. What are these glands called?

explanation.summary: Brunner's glands secrete protective alkaline mucus in the proximal duodenum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies Brunner's glands in the submucosa of the proximal duodenum, secreting alkaline mucus in response to acid and secretin as part of mucosal defense.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oxyntic (gastric) glands contain acid-secreting parietal cells in the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Peyer's patches are lymphoid tissue for immune surveillance, not alkaline mucus secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Crypts of Lieberkuhn are intestinal glands housing stem and secretory cells, not the submucosal alkaline glands described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Goblet cells secrete mucus but are individual epithelial cells, not the submucosal glands specified.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: A child with recurrent respiratory infections has failure to thrive and steatorrhea. Even though secretin release from S cells is intact, defective ductal secretion prevents alkaline pancreatic fluid from reaching the duodenum. Which protein is dysfunctional?

explanation.summary: Cystic fibrosis results from defective CFTR, blocking ductal chloride/bicarbonate secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states CFTR mutations (commonly delta-F508) prevent ductal chloride and bicarbonate secretion even when secretin release is intact, so alkaline fluid never reaches the duodenum.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbonic anhydrase supplies bicarbonate substrate but the defect described is the CFTR chloride channel.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Na-K-ATPase maintains ion gradients generally and is not the mutated protein in this disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CCK-A receptors mediate acinar enzyme secretion, unrelated to the ductal bicarbonate defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secretin receptors are intact here; the problem is downstream ductal CFTR function.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: CCK-induced gallbladder contraction delivers bile salts into the duodenum during fat digestion. What is the primary role of these bile salts?

explanation.summary: Bile salts emulsify dietary fats, increasing surface area for lipase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states bile salts are essential for emulsifying dietary fats, dramatically increasing the surface area available for lipase activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydrolysis of triglycerides is performed by lipase; bile salts emulsify but do not hydrolyze.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutralization of acid is the role of pancreatic and Brunner's-gland bicarbonate, not bile salts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Trypsinogen is activated by enterokinase, not bile salts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Amino acid absorption occurs via enterocyte transporters, not bile salts.

questions.topicName: GI Hormones & the Intestinal Phase of Digestion
questions.stem: In addition to stimulating pancreatic bicarbonate secretion, secretin dampens the gastric phase of acid secretion. By which action does secretin reduce gastric acid output?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stimulating gastrin release from G cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Suppressing gastrin release from G cells

explanation.summary: Secretin suppresses gastrin release from G cells and reduces parietal cell acid output.
